title: QUIC Simulator-Backed Correctness Scenario Architecture
purpose: Define how the repository tracks simulator-backed network-condition scenarios as requirement-linked correctness evidence without turning the simulator itself into a support oracle.
design_summary: The simulator-backed lane is a scenario registry and evidence model layered over existing QUIC requirements. Each scenario records a stable scenario id, classification, upstream simulator profile, upstream source reference, concrete simulator parameters, local role, peer shape, mapped requirement ids or accounting-only anchor, expected observable result, evidence bundle, status, and promotion rule. Correctness scenarios must point back to RFC, CRT, or INT requirements; advisory interop scenarios remain characterization surfaces until separate verification promotes a bounded requirement claim; performance-only scenarios remain separate and route through benchmark reporting. The first helper surface is intentionally narrow: it can plan and evidence only `SIM-QUIC-BASE-0001` and `SIM-QUIC-LOSS-0001` while preserving simulator invocation metadata under `artifacts/network-simulator`. Passing a simulator run promotes only the bounded mapped requirement claim, not broad implementation support.
alternatives_considered: Treat every successful simulator run as broad support proof. Rejected because the simulator creates network conditions but does not define the protocol assertion being proven.

Create one requirement per raw network parameter value such as 10 percent loss or 50 ms delay. Rejected because the normative behavior is the QUIC rule; parameter values belong in verification scenarios unless a product support tier intentionally adopts them as guarantees.
Keep simulator planning only in free-form docs. Rejected because scenario status and promotion rules need stable requirement, work-item, and verification links.
Make the first simulator lane a blocking CI gate. Rejected until setup cost, image drift, evidence stability, and failure classification are understood.
edge_cases_and_constraints: A scenario classification must be correctness, advisory-interop, or performance-only.
A scenario status can be planned, implemented, passing, failing, blocked, flaky, or performance-only.
Scenario evidence must preserve logs, runner reports when applicable, qlog, packet captures, simulator stdout, and the exact simulator profile parameters.
Scenario evidence must preserve the upstream simulator source reference or pinned commit/path used to interpret the profile parameters.
A performance-only result must not be used as correctness proof unless it also checks the mapped protocol behavior.
Interop peer failures, simulator infrastructure failures, and Incursa-side failures must remain distinguishable.
Simulator settings are evidence inputs, requirement statements are the normative claims, and verification artifacts are the proof record.
The first implementation should be manual and advisory until evidence stability is demonstrated.
The first helper surface must not introduce runtime transport changes, hosted workflow dispatch, or broad scenario matrix expansion.
data_and_state_considerations: Scenario definitions are planned in documentation and canonical verification artifacts. Execution evidence should be written under `artifacts/network-simulator/<scenario-id>/<run-id>/` or an equivalent uploaded artifact root. The first helper writes a scenario summary, invocation log, simulator stdout/stderr, artifact tree, optional staged endpoint Docker contexts, and optional docker-compose override file before any later qlog/pcap analysis is claimed. Generated summaries can later be added under `specs/generated/quic/` once the scenario schema is implemented.
risks: Readers may confuse a network-condition scenario with a formal support tier if promotion language is too broad.
Simulator image or upstream scenario drift can change results without source changes in this repository.
Random drop and corruption profiles can introduce flakiness unless deterministic droplist or repeated-run policy is defined for proof-grade cases.
Large matrices can become expensive before the first few scenarios prove diagnostic value.

supplemental_sections.heading: Scenario Fields
supplemental_sections.content: Each scenario should carry `scenario_id`, `classification`, `upstream_profile`, `upstream_reference`, `parameters`, `local_role`, `peer_shape`, `mapped_requirements`, `expected_observables`, `evidence_required`, `status`, and `promotion_rule`. Correctness rows require mapped protocol requirements before promotion. Advisory and performance-only rows may use `REQ-QUIC-INT-0026` as the accounting anchor, but their promotion rule must say that no protocol correctness claim is promoted.

supplemental_sections.heading: Initial Scenario Families
supplemental_sections.content: The initial planning families are baseline point-to-point transfer, deterministic packet loss, bounded blackhole/PTO recovery, deterministic reordering, corruption discard behavior, rebind or migration characterization, and TCP or UDP cross-traffic. The first implementation wave should stop at baseline point-to-point and deterministic packet loss until evidence stability is demonstrated. Helper-owned endpoint staging may prepare Incursa.Quic client/server build contexts, mounted source/download/certificate roots, and compose overrides for those two scenarios only. Only the scenarios mapped to explicit requirements count as correctness proof.
